name: XBRL Tagging and Regulatory Filing
title: XBRL Tagging and Regulatory Filing
answer: XBRL tagging is the practice of attaching machine-readable labels to individual facts in financial statements and related disclosures, so that a regulator, an analyst, or a software system can pull a specific number without parsing a PDF. It sits inside financial reporting and synthesis, where the output of the accounting close meets the filing requirements of a securities regulator. The work covers primary financial statements, footnotes, and increasingly non-financial disclosures such as ESG metrics. A tagging specialist, a financial reporting manager, or an external filing agent may all perform the task. The scope stops at the boundary of the filing itself, though the tagged data often feeds downstream analysis and surveillance.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: XBRL tagging is the practice of attaching machine-readable labels to individual facts in financial statements and related disclosures, so that a regulator, an analyst, or a software system can pull a specific number without parsing a PDF. It sits inside financial reporting and synthesis, where the output of the accounting close meets the filing requirements of a securities regulator. The work covers primary financial statements, footnotes, and increasingly non-financial disclosures such as ESG metrics. A tagging specialist, a financial reporting manager, or an external filing agent may all perform the task. The scope stops at the boundary of the filing itself, though the tagged data often feeds downstream analysis and surveillance.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The core infrastructure is a taxonomy, a structured dictionary of concepts with definitions, labels, and relationships, published by a standards body or a regulator. A filing is built as an instance document, which pairs each tagged fact with a context, a unit, and a period. Software for tagging ranges from desktop add-ins for spreadsheet and word processing programs to enterprise disclosure management platforms. The filing then travels through a regulator's electronic submission system, such as the SEC's EDGAR, which validates the instance against the taxonomy and business rules before acceptance. Validation tools check calculations, dimensions, and consistency across statements.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with a mapping exercise, where each line item and disclosure in the draft financial statements is matched to the closest standard taxonomy concept. Where no standard concept fits, the preparer creates an extension element, which must be anchored to a standard concept and documented. Tagging is then applied in the authoring tool, with dates, units, and dimensions set for every fact. A review pass checks that the tagged data agrees with the human-readable document, that calculations tie, and that prior-period comparatives are consistent. The final step is a validation run against the regulator's rules, followed by submission and, if needed, correction.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on accuracy, liability, and the provenance of each tag. The preparer is responsible for the tagged data even when a third-party agent or software vendor performs the mechanical work, and the audit trail must show who created, changed, and approved each tag. Version control matters because taxonomies change annually and a filing may be amended. Provenance includes the taxonomy release, the extension documentation, and the validation log. Poor tagging can trigger regulatory comment, restatement, or loss of safe harbor for forward-looking statements, so internal controls over financial reporting usually extend to the tagging process.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward inline XBRL, where tags are embedded in the human-readable document itself, reducing the need for separate instance files. Regulators in several jurisdictions are expanding digital tagging to ESG, climate, and other non-financial disclosures, which raises new questions about materiality and comparability. AI-assisted tagging is emerging, using language models to suggest concepts and detect anomalies, but human review remains the control point. Over time, the expectation is that tagged data will be consumed directly by analysts, auditors, and supervisors, making the quality of the tag as important as the number it carries.
